title: Everyday Greetings
introduction: Greet people through the day and say good night. These common forms are useful starting points; local greetings also vary.
summary: You practised morning, afternoon and evening greetings, and a good-night farewell.

exercises.prompt: It is 8 a.m. and you meet a neighbour outside. Choose the common good-morning expression.
exercises.explanation: Ụtụtụ ọma means good morning. Communities also use other morning greetings.

exercises.prompt: You arrive for a friendly visit after lunch. Which time-of-day greeting fits the afternoon?
exercises.explanation: Ehihie ọma is a common good-afternoon expression.

exercises.prompt: It is evening and you meet a friend for a chat. Which greeting fits this time of day?
exercises.explanation: Mgbede ọma means good evening. It greets someone rather than ends a bedtime conversation.

exercises.prompt: After the evening chat, you and your friend are going to bed. Choose a good-night farewell.
exercises.explanation: Ka chi foo is a good-night expression, a wish for day to break.

title: Introduce Yourself
introduction: Introduce your name, ask someone else’s name and share a little about yourself.
summary: You practised exchanging names, saying you are a student and saying you speak Igbo.

exercises.prompt: You join a new study group. Your name is Ada. Choose your introduction.
exercises.explanation: Aha m bụ ... introduces your name. Here the name is Ada.

exercises.prompt: A new classmate has greeted you but has not said their name. How do you ask it?
exercises.explanation: Kedụ aha gị? asks what your name is. Gị means your here.

exercises.prompt: At a campus event, someone asks about you. Choose the statement that says you are a student.
exercises.explanation: M bụ nwa akwụkwọ means I am a student.

exercises.prompt: During an introduction, a friend says “M na-asụ Igbo.” What have they told you?
exercises.explanation: M na-asụ Igbo means I speak Igbo. The speaker is describing a language they speak.

title: Family & People
introduction: Introduce a parent or friend and understand who someone is talking about in their family.
summary: You practised introducing your mother, naming your father or friend and recognising a reference to both parents.

exercises.prompt: Your mother joins you while you are chatting with a friend. Choose the statement that introduces her.
exercises.explanation: Nke a bụ nne m means this is my mother.

exercises.prompt: Your father’s name is Obi. A visitor asks his name. Which statement answers them?
exercises.explanation: Aha nna m bụ Obi means my father’s name is Obi.

exercises.prompt: A friend mentions “Nne m na nna m” when talking about who is visiting. Who are they talking about?
exercises.explanation: Nne m na nna m means my mother and my father. Na joins the two people here.

exercises.prompt: You are talking about your friend Ada to someone who has not met her. Choose the statement that gives your friend’s name.
exercises.explanation: Aha enyi m bụ Ada means my friend’s name is Ada.

title: Food & Drink
introduction: At a friend’s home, express hunger or thirst, talk about cooking and wish someone an enjoyable meal.
summary: You practised saying you are hungry or thirsty, describing cooking and wishing someone an enjoyable meal.

exercises.prompt: You have not eaten yet. Your host asks how you feel. Choose the expression that says you are hungry.
exercises.explanation: Agụụ na-agụ m means I am hungry. It tells your host that you need food.

exercises.prompt: After a walk, you need a drink rather than food. What can you say to your host?
exercises.explanation: Mmiri na-agụ m means I am thirsty. Mmiri is water.

exercises.prompt: A friend finds you in the kitchen and asks what you are doing. Choose the statement that says you are cooking food.
exercises.explanation: M na-esi nri means I am cooking food.

exercises.prompt: Your friend is about to eat the meal you have shared. Choose the expression that wishes them an enjoyable meal.
exercises.explanation: Rie nke ọma is used to wish someone an enjoyable meal.
